Atresmedia’s new slate aims to address this by focusing on projects with stronger market potential. SCIENCE · ScienceDaily · editor 9/10 · 1 min read fact-checked

Caffeine Disrupts Deep Sleep Even Without Delaying Onset

Recent research indicates that caffeine consumption can compromise the restorative quality of sleep, even if it does not prevent individuals from falling asleep or reduce the total time spent in bed. Studies using EEG recordings have revealed that caffeine intake is associated with a reduction in slow brain waves, which are critical for deep sleep.

The findings suggest that the negative impact of caffeine is not limited to sleep latency or duration. Instead, it affects the structural integrity of sleep cycles, specifically diminishing the deep sleep phase that is essential for physical recovery and cognitive restoration. This means that a person may feel they have had a full night’s rest, yet their brain may not have achieved the necessary deep sleep stages.

Individual sensitivity to caffeine varies dramatically among people. For some, consuming caffeine earlier in the day can still affect nighttime recovery. This variability highlights the complexity of caffeine’s half-life and its interaction with individual metabolic rates. The research underscores that “being awake” is not the only metric for sleep quality; the depth and restorative capacity of sleep are equally important.

The study emphasizes that the timing of caffeine consumption is not the sole determinant of its impact. Even if a person falls asleep normally and stays in bed for eight hours, the presence of caffeine may alter the brain’s electrical activity, leading to less restorative sleep. This has implications for daily habits, as many people rely on caffeine for energy without considering its downstream effects on sleep architecture.

What to watch: Further research into personalized caffeine sensitivity and its specific effects on sleep stages.

A Sri Lankan court has delivered a significant verdict in the case involving the Easter Sunday attacks, convicting 14 accused individuals. The men were charged with aiding and abetting the suicide bombers responsible for the devastating strikes.

The attacks, which occurred on April 21, 2019, targeted three luxury hotels and three churches across the country. The coordinated bombings resulted in the deaths of 279 people, marking one of the deadliest terror incidents in the nation’s modern history.

In addition to the 14 convictions, a 15th defendant was found guilty of only some of the charges leveled against him. The court also acquitted nine other accused individuals, clearing them of the charges in this particular phase of the trial.

Bombay High Court Rules in Favor of Dharma Productions in GST Dispute

Dharma Productions has secured a significant legal victory in a tax dispute with the Bombay High Court. The production house won a case involving a tax demand of Rs. 12.11 crores related to the licensing of copyright in its cinematographic films.

The core of the dispute centered on how the delivery of film content should be classified for tax purposes. The court quashed the tax demand, finding that the mere electronic delivery of film content could not, by itself, justify its classification as “Information Technology Software.” This distinction is crucial, as it affects the applicable tax rates and obligations for the entertainment industry.

The bench’s decision highlights the importance of accurate classification of digital media services. By rejecting the notion that film copyright licensing is equivalent to IT software, the court has provided clarity for similar cases within the sector. This ruling may have broader implications for how digital content distribution is taxed in India, potentially offering relief to other production companies facing similar categorization challenges.

The case underscores the ongoing regulatory debates surrounding the intersection of traditional media rights and modern digital delivery mechanisms. Dharma Productions’ win serves as a precedent for the correct treatment of film copyrights in tax assessments.

What to watch: Future legal challenges regarding the tax classification of other digital media services.
